newsitem.title: USA: U.S. plays down consequences of Deng's death.
newsitem.headline: U.S. plays down consequences of Deng's death.

text.p: U.S. officials on Wednesday played down concerns over the death of China's elder statesman Deng Xiaoping, saying he had been off the political stage for years and a transition of power had already taken place.

Both administration officials and private analysts said the death of the 93-year-old Chinese patriarch would be unlikely to make much impact on the Chinese political scene, where his successors seem firmly in control.

"It's been clear to everybody observing the Chinese scene that they've been undergoing a transition of sorts," said State Department spokesman Glyn Davies, speaking before reports of Deng's death were officially confirmed.
"There has been transition, not just economically but a political transition in terms of China's leadership."
A White House official, who asked not to be identified, put it more emphatically.
"The important thing to remember is that there will be no political convulsions in China ... as might have been the case several years ago, because the transition has already happened," he said.
"(President) Jiang Zemin is in the captain's seat."

A senior State Department official said Deng "had in recent years detached himself from the day-to-day levers of power, was no longer making decisions, clearly. So as regards the functioning of China this will likely not have a great effect."

But the official said this was "an important moment" for the Chinese because Deng had been a seminal figure in China's communist revolution and, more recently, the architect of the country's economic reforms.

Deng, whose death came just days before a scheduled visit to Beijing by new U.S. Secretary of State Madeleine Albright, retired from his last official position in 1990 and has not been seen in public for the last three years.
Nicholas Lardy, a China specialist at the Brookings Institution in Washington, said he shared the administration's assessment.

He said Deng's absence from the political scene made him different from other leaders in the past, such as President Tito of Yugoslavia and Francisco Franco in Spain, whose deaths after long illnesses led to profound changes. Lardy added:
"One cannot in the last two years point to any central decision in which Deng had a role. It is hard to see how his absence would have much of an effect in any policy issue."
While China faces critical political and economic choices in the medium term, these would have loomed with or without Deng, Lardy and other analysts said.

David Bachman, chair of the China studies department at the University of Washington in Seattle, said: "For all practical policital purposes Deng has been dead for about a year anyway -- too weak and too ill to have any important role in Chinese politics."
Nevertheless he said the Chinese leadership would act carefully over the next six months, particular ahead of the party Congress in the fall.
And one analyst in Washington sounded a note of caution, saying the best-laid transition plans could come unstuck, and that one unpredictable factor was popular reaction in China.
"The aspiration of the Chinese for political reform was one question that was not resolved by Deng," he said.

The United States has every reason to hope for continued stability in China as the world's most populous nation struggles to reconcile its communist political system with its booming, semi-capitalist economy.

Apart from the security dangers of a serious power struggle in Beijing, Washington is trying to keep on course a policy that seeks to combine human rights concerns with continued "engagement" with a major trade partner.

In the teeth of much criticism from Congress, the Clinton administration has increasingly subordinated human rights to engagement and Albright, who took over as secretary of state last month, has shown no sign of changing tack.

Her decision to include Beijing in her inaugural foreign tour -- which is basically confined to key allies in Europe and Asia -- sends an unmistakeable signal of how far China has risen in Washington's scale of priorities.
U.S. officials said they expected the Beijing visit, set for Feb. 24, to go ahead despite Deng's death.
